t.3.4.1: Having slain in the forest that rākṣasa Virādha of fearsome strength, the valiant Rāma then embraced Sītā and comforted her, and spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa of blazing splendor.
t.3.4.2: This forest is harsh and hard to pass through, and we are not used to roaming in forests. Let us go quickly to Śarabhaṅga, whose wealth is his austerity.
t.3.4.3: Rāghava went to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
t.3.4.4: Near Śarabhaṅga, who possessed godlike power and whose self had been purified by austerity, he beheld a great wonder.
t.3.4.5: He beheld the lord of the gods, resplendent in his form, like the sun and the fire, not touching the earth.
t.3.4.6: He saw the god, adorned with brilliantly shining ornaments and wearing spotless garments, being worshipped by many great-souled beings like himself.
t.3.4.7: Not far from him he saw a chariot yoked with bay horses, poised in the sky and shining like the newly risen sun.
t.3.4.8: He saw a spotless parasol, resembling a dense mass of pale white clouds and like the disc of the moon, adorned with garlands of varied flowers.
t.3.4.10: Gandharvas, immortals and Siddhas, along with many supreme sages, praised with excellent words the god who stood in the sky.
t.3.4.9: He saw also two excellent, very costly chowrie-fans with golden handles, held by two forest maidens and being waved over his head.
t.3.4.11: Seeing Śatakratu there, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa: "Those divine steeds of Śakra Puruhūta, moving through the sky, of which we heard long ago, these bay horses are surely they."
t.3.4.13: On the chests of all of them hang necklaces gleaming like fire; O Saumitri, they bear the form of youths twenty-five years of age.
t.3.4.12: And these, O tiger among men, who stand all around the chariot, hundreds upon hundreds of young men wearing earrings, with swords in their hands...
t.3.4.14: For this, they say, is ever the age of the gods, just as these tigers among men appear, so pleasing to behold.
t.3.4.15: Lakṣmaṇa, stay right here with Vaidehī for a moment, until I clearly learn who this radiant one in the chariot is.
t.3.4.16: Having thus spoken to Saumitri, "Let it be stayed right here," Kākutstha approached toward the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
t.3.4.17: Then the lord of Śacī, seeing Rāma approaching, took leave of Śarabhaṅga and spoke these words to the gods.
t.3.4.18: That Rāma is approaching here; before he speaks to me, bring the matter to its conclusion, and after that he may see me.
t.3.4.19: Before long I shall see him victorious and with his purpose accomplished, for a great deed is to be done by him, one exceedingly hard for others to achieve.
t.3.4.20: Having thus taken leave of him and having honored the ascetic, the wielder of the thunderbolt, subduer of foes, went to heaven in a chariot yoked with bay horses.
t.3.4.21: When the thousand-eyed one had departed, Rāghava, together with his retinue, approached Śarabhaṅga, who was seated performing the agnihotra fire-offering.
t.3.4.22: Rāma, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa clasped his feet, and then, with his permission, they sat down, having been granted a dwelling and invited to stay.
t.3.4.24: O Rāma, this granter of boons wishes to lead me to the world of Brahmā, which I have won by fierce austerity and which is hard to attain for those of undisciplined self.
t.3.4.23: Then that Rāghava asked about Śakra's visit, and Śarabhaṅga related all of it to Rāghava.
t.3.4.25: O tiger among men, having learned that you were dwelling not far away, I will not go to the world of Brahmā without having seen you, my beloved guest.
t.3.4.26: Having met you, I shall go to the heaven frequented by the gods. O tiger among men, I have won imperishable and auspicious worlds, both those of Brahmā and those on the vault of heaven; accept these worlds of mine.
t.3.4.27: Thus addressed by the sage Śarabhaṅga, Rāghava, a tiger among men and skilled in all the śāstras, spoke these words.
t.3.4.29: Thus addressed by Rāghava, whose strength was equal to Śakra's, the greatly wise Śarabhaṅga spoke these words once again.
t.3.4.28: I myself shall win all the worlds, O great sage; but I wish for a dwelling place to be shown to me here in the forest.
t.3.4.30: Go to the ascetic Sutīkṣṇa, who dwells in a pure place, in a delightful region of the forest; he will arrange a dwelling for you.
t.3.4.31: This is the path, O tiger among men; watch me for a moment, dear one, while I cast off my limbs as a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.
t.3.4.32: Then the greatly radiant Śarabhaṅga, knower of the mantras, having kindled the fire and made an offering into it with clarified butter, entered the fire.
t.3.4.33: The fire burned the body hair and the locks of that great-souled one, his aged skin, his bones as well, and whatever flesh and blood there was.
t.3.4.34: And he became a youth resembling fire; rising up from that pyre, Śarabhaṅga shone forth.
t.3.4.35: Passing beyond the worlds of those who maintain the sacred fires, of the great-souled seers, and of the gods, he ascended to the world of Brahmā.
t.3.4.36: In that world, that bull among the twice-born, of meritorious deeds, beheld the Grandsire together with his attendants. And the Grandsire too, seeing that twice-born one, rejoiced and said, "A hearty welcome to you!"
